- Model consistently underestimates prices in the early part of the forecast horizon, especially after recent spikes or corrections.
- Overestimates prices in the final 5–10 days of the forecast, particularly when true prices show strong upward momentum or mean reversion.
- Tends to lag behind true price movements by 1–3 days, especially in downward trends — forecasts dip too early or too slowly.
- Overreacts to short-term volatility: spikes in history trigger exaggerated overshoots in forecast, then undercorrects later.
- Mean reversion bias: model assumes prices return to historical averages too quickly, missing sustained trends.
- Forecasts often underestimate the magnitude of upward price shocks, especially when preceded by low prices or strong policy signals.
- When history includes a recent high, model tends to overpredict a subsequent low — fails to recognize the “high-low” reversal pattern.
- Forecasts are more accurate when the last 5–7 days of history show stable or trending prices, but fail when history is volatile or contains multiple reversals.
